newsitem.title: USA: U.S. crudes end weaker on heavy futures sales.
newsitem.headline: U.S. crudes end weaker on heavy futures sales.

text.p: Heavy selling on the NYMEX futures market worked to depress the value of outright cash crudes in the United States on Tuesday.
Cash markets were also down in the domestic grades, pressured by active selling in the main Louisiana sweet market by a major U.S. refiner, traders said.
Outrights pushed lower all session, deflated by the return of Iraqi crude oil to world markets -- even if they were delayed by technical glitches -- and heavy technical selling.
Products futures also worked to unseat the crude price, with negative inventory data released late in the day.
January West Texas Intermediate/Cushing ended around 85 cents lower at $24.35-$24.45 a barrel.
Grades featured declining values for Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James, which sold at 80 cts over the Jan WTI, down some 8-10 cts from the end of business on Monday.
"We had refiners in selling the LLS all day," said a trader, who echoed market sentiment that foreign barrels have finally become less of an economic disaster zone.

Firmer prices for Dated Brent and CFD's indicated the new opening in arbitrage for the transatlantic cargoes. A wet Brent loading Dec 21-23 sold at Jan Brent +33 cts, 11 cts higher than the previous deal seen on Monday.
Traders also said a major U.S. trader was preparing to bring over a fresh Brent cargo.
Other grade activity saw West Texas Sour/Midland remain at around $1.90 below the Jan WTI, surprising some players who forecast even weaker levels with the return of Iraqi crude.
Apparent technical problems with electrical equipment at Kirkuk delayed the pumping of Iraq oil. Turkish officials said there was no oil pumped into the Ceyhan terminal Tuesday.

U.N. oil overseers rejected the second contract submitted under the oil-for-food deal as well, citing technical problems in the manner the contract was submitted by the Iraqi State Oil Marketing Organization.
U.N. sources said the contract was between Elf Aquitaine and Iraq, following the first contract submitted with Turkey's Tupras oil company for 75,000 barrels per day of supply.
